text: Does Jeremiah 10 condemn Christmas
trees? Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen.
I'm a scholar of the Bible and religion.
And every time I start making videos
about a lot of the misinformation in
circulation about Christmas, the origin
of Christmas, the origin of December
25th, the origin of Christmas trees,
inevitably I get somebody asking about
Jeremiah 10. Let's take a look at the
passage. This is the updated edition of
the New Revised Standard Version. For
the customs of the peoples are false. A
tree from the forest is cut down and
worked with an axe by the hands of an
artisan. They deck it with silver and
gold. They fasten it with hammers and
nails so that it cannot move. Their
idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber
field and they cannot speak. They have
to be carried for they cannot walk. Do
not be afraid of them for they cannot do
evil nor is it in them to do good. And a
lot of people seem to think that the
tradition that is being referred to in
verses 3 and four is the cutting down of
a tree to bring it inside and decorate
it and either worship it or just use it
as part of a celebration and perhaps a
winter celebration. So the idea seems to
be either that this witnesses to an
ancient non-Jewish tradition of bringing
trees indoors and decorating them or it
might be referring to something else but
prophetically it is condemning the use
of the Christmas tree. Neither of these
things is true. This is about cutting
down a tree to use the wood to create an
idol. Now, here's the Hebrew of this
passage, and I want to talk in a little
more detail about what's going on in
here, just because the translation makes
it a little harder to understand. The uh
far left of the second line down, the
last four words are maad,
and that is translated in the NRSVE,
worked with an axe, by the hands of an
artisan. And literally, it is the work
of the hands of an artisan with tools.
And so those tools might be an axe,
could be something else. So some people
think this just is a reference to
cutting down the tree, but it's very
clearly not. It is a reference to the
working of the wood into the shape of
whatever the divine image is going to
be, whether that is anthropomorphic
or something else. The first step for
the creation of a divine image in the
ancient world, whether that's Syria,
Palestine or Assyria or Egypt is to get
wood which usually served as the core of
the divine image. And certain types of
wood were considered best for that. In
fact, in ancient Mesopotamia, the
tamarisque tree was so commonly used as
the core of a divine image that that
type of wood was referred to as the
empty eli or the bone of the gods
because it formed the internal part of
the divine image. Then we go on to verse
four and in the nrsvue we see they deck
it with silver and gold. Now, if we go
to the Hebrew, it says in silver and
gold they beautify it. And some people
think, oh, this is like uh decorations,
tinsel. We're throwing silver and gold
tinsel all over or we're decorating it
with uh globes or whatever, stars. And
the reality is that this is a reference
to covering the core of the divine image
in silver and gold plating. Because
normally the divine image was supposed
to be made of a combination of a wood
core and then usually gold or silver
exterior because that was considered
appropriate material to represent the
divine being. And if you would like a
discussion of how divine images were
made in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt,
here are a handful of wonderful texts
you can go check out. I also discuss it
in my book Adoniz Divine Images which is
open access. You can find it through my
link tree. And this chapter discusses
how divine images were made, how divine
images were encountered and goes through
the fact that they usually had a wooden
core and then uh an outside that was
made of precious metals like silver and
gold. So this is about a divine image.
Now next in verse four, as we see in the
NRSVU, it says they fasten it with
hammers and nails so that it cannot
move. Now a lot of people imagine that
this indicates this is a tree because
they've got to hold it upright otherwise
it'll fall down and that's not what's
going on here. If you look in other idol
palemic passages in Deuter instance you
see that divine images one of the ways
they're mocked is by the fact that they
topple over that you have to be careful
to make sure they are standing upright
because they are intended to stand
upright. So here the idea is they're
using a hammer and nails to ensure that
it is fixed in place that it does not
topple over. And the next indication
that this is definitely talking about
divine images and not talking about some
decorated tree is that the next verse
quite explicitly refers to divine
images. The beginning of verse 5, their
idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber
field and they cannot speak. They have
to be carried for they cannot walk. Do
not be afraid of them for they cannot do
evil. nor is it in them to do good. So
this is rhetoric that is condemning the
use of divine images. A tree was chopped
down so that the wood could be worked
into whatever shape the core of this
divine image was going to take. That
involved removing the branches, removing
the bark, shaping it into the shape they
wanted and then applying the silver and
gold and other types of overlays to it.
So this is not about a tree that is
being decorated and brought indoors.
This is about divine images. This has
nothing to do with Christmas trees.
There was no such tradition in this time
or this place. And this is not something
that is prophetically looking forward to
the use of the Christmas tree. Jeremiah
10 absolutely is not condemning
Christmas trees. And the fit for this
